correctness.rationale: For all integers 2<=p<=q, a total dominating set is precisely an incidence edge set not covered by any mixed row-column pair, because adjacency requires both coordinates to differ. A three-edge matching is a minimal witness. Without one, Koenig matching-cover duality forces a same-side two-vertex cover; direct testing shows minimality exactly when two edges occur on each of the two supporting rows or columns. These three configurations exhaust all cases. Inclusion-exclusion of two-by-two rectangle overlaps gives the precise coefficients. The code exhaustively enumerated all graph subsets on 11 finite instances, including the 18-vertex K_3 x K_6, and agreed. Finite tests corroborate but do not replace the all-parameters proof.

originality.rationale: Compared the exact set polynomial and its upper/WTD implications against the known 2012 minimum scalar theorem, the 2016 two-row upper theorem plus its explicit general question, the 2020 WTD study, and the 2021 ordinary domination-polynomial result for these very same products. The main new assertion is the full minimal total dominating set classification and labeled census, rather than an already known scalar or a special case of ordinary domination; the k=1 upper corollary does not follow from the previously inspected proofs. Search coverage leaves explicit literature-priority risk.
residual_risks: Some publisher-hosted full-text interfaces are inaccessible, although relevant transcriptions and authorized open versions were inspected where available.
An unindexed or differently labeled exact polynomial or a more recent theorem proving the 2016 upper-total product question could overlap; negative indexed searches are not uniqueness proofs.
This is a self-review and not independent validation.

value.rationale: The result counts every inclusion-minimal total dominating set across an infinite and naturally occurring graph family, and gives a sharp transition at factor order two. Its three-matching/two-row structural dichotomy supplies reusable insight rather than a raw small table. The all-factor upper equality settles the k=1 instance of Kazemi’s explicitly posed 2016 question. Neither minimum domination scalar, ordinary domination polynomial, nor previous two-row upper result determines the full census.
